title: NCHAR Data Type & NCHAR vs CHAR
description: Learn how to use the NCHAR data type to store fixed-length, Unicode character strings.

data.text: The NCHAR data type stores fixed-length, Unicode character string data. Use NCHAR when you need to store Unicode characters such as Japanese, Korean, or Chinese.

data.title: NCHAR Syntax
data.content: Defines an NCHAR column with a specified length.

data.text: n specifies the string length from 1 to 4,000. The storage size is two times n bytes.

rows: Storage equals double the size specified

data.text: Note that you must prefix Unicode character string constants with the letter N. Otherwise, SQL Server will convert the string to the default code page which may not recognize certain Unicode characters.

data.alt: SQL Server NCHAR data type example output

data.text: Without the `N` prefix, a string literal is first interpreted using the code page of the current collation. If that code page cannot represent a character, SQL Server silently replaces it with a question mark. The script below shows the difference using a CJK character that a Latin code page cannot store.

data.title: Unicode literals need the N prefix
data.content: The plain literal is mangled by the database code page; the N-prefixed literal is preserved. Storing supplementary characters such as emoji also needs an SC collation.

data.title: Common mistake
data.text: Forgetting the N prefix is one of the most common globalization bugs. It can also defeat an index: comparing an nvarchar column with a non-Unicode literal forces a conversion that turns an index seek into a scan.

data.title: NCHAR Key Points
points: NCHAR stores fixed-length, Unicode character strings.
Use NCHAR for Unicode data like Japanese, Korean, or Chinese characters.
NCHAR uses 2 bytes per character vs. 1 byte for CHAR.
Maximum length is 4,000 characters (vs. 8,000 for CHAR).
Prefix Unicode strings with N for proper handling.
